Apple has submitted its proposal regarding the fees charged for transactions outside the App Store system in the Epic Games lawsuit. Here are the relevant details.

Apple submits proposal for commissions on transactions outside the App Store

After multiple requests to stay the district court proceedings—which will determine whether and how Apple can charge fees for transactions outside its IAP system within the App Store—Apple has finally submitted its proposal, outlining the suggested fee structure.

Apple's submission of its proposal comes right after the Supreme Court denied Apple's request to stay the lower court proceedings. Apple had hoped to stay the relevant proceedings so that the Supreme Court could review its case, in which it may be held in contempt of court for charging a 27% commission on transactions outside the App Store. Previously, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers had issued an injunction requiring Apple to allow developers to direct users to alternative purchasing methods.

Apple argued both in the district court and subsequently in the Supreme Court that the court's ruling could affect the outcome of the fee determination process, and therefore the relevant proceedings should be stayed pending the court's decision. However, the Supreme Court denied Apple's request, allowing the district court proceedings to continue while the review is underway.

Accordingly, Apple has now submitted its proposal, with the suggested fees as follows:

Standard apps charged at 15% (such apps currently subject to a 30% in-app purchase ("IAP") commission);

Apple stated: "The factual and expert evidence regarding the above proposed commission rates has also been submitted concurrently." The company added:

Apple further pointed out that its "proposed outside link commissions can also be compared with those of other competing app stores," including Google Play, Samsung Galaxy Store, and Amazon's Android App Marketplace.

The company also noted: "The standard outside link fee structure for the Google Play Store is: standard rate 20%, program rate 15%, subscription rate 10%—rates which Epic has also agreed to."

Apple stated that it still believes the fee determination process should be stayed pending the outcome of the Supreme Court case, and added that the submission of this proposal is solely to comply with Judge Gonzalez Rogers's instructions.

The company also pointed out that the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals has overturned the district court's comprehensive injunction on commissions for outside link transactions, and stated that such commissions would only pose a problem if they effectively constitute a backdoor ban.

Following Apple's submission of its proposal, Epic may now respond, and Apple is expected to submit its arguments to the Supreme Court by September 14.
